title: Assessing the Covid-19 infodemic and misinformation among university students in Morocco
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 295 Moroccan university students (8 March - 9 May 2021) giving two shares with explicit denominators: 269/295 (91.2%) who say they came across COVID-19 misinformation during the pandemic (RECALL exposure) and 36.3% who report having transmitted misinformation at least once (RECALL sharing).

estimates.platform: any source (respondents named social media, online news outlets, television and family/friends)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they came across misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic
estimates.denominator: 295 university students across Morocco who completed an online questionnaire distributed to faculties and online student groups (303 received, 8 excluded)
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to whether they encountered misinformation during the pandemic; no time window narrower than 'during the pandemic' and no verification of the content named
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; the paper treats misinformation as false COVID-19 claims, illustrated by respondent examples such as "The Covid-19 vaccine has been tainted with man-made HIV" and "It's pointless wearing a mask"
estimates.source_quote: The majority of respondents 269/295 (91.2%) claimed to have come across misinformation during the pandemic. The main source of misinformation was online news outlets.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report of having encountered misinformation; authors later categorised the free-text examples by subject but did not verify the claims. Questionnaire pre-tested on 10 respondents; no inter-coder reliability reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: For misinformation, respondents were asked to indicate whether or not they encountered misinformation during the pandemic, where they came across such information and how often, on a Likert scale from one to five, they found themselves involved in misinformation.
estimates.notes: population_scope coded 'other' because the sample is university students only, not a general-public sample. No platform is attached to the item, which asks about the pandemic period as a whole, so platform_norm is survey.

estimates.value_raw: 36.3% (complement of 63.7% who reported never transmitting misinformation; the Abstract states 36.6%)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report having transmitted misinformation at least once during the pandemic
estimates.denominator: 295 university students across Morocco who completed the online questionnaire
estimates.definition: Respondent placed themselves above 'never' on a 1-5 Likert frequency scale asking how often they found themselves involved in transmitting information that proved to be false
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given; misinformation is 'information that proved to be false' in the respondent's own judgement
estimates.source_quote: On the question of having transmitted information that proved to be false, the majority of respondents (63.7%) reported having never transmitting misinformation. In other words, some 36.3% of respondents were involved in transmitting misinformation at some point during the pandemic.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported frequency on a five-point Likert scale; no verification of what was transmitted.
estimates.moderator_quote: how often, on a Likert scale from one to five, they found themselves involved in misinformation
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL: the paper reports the same quantity twice with different values - 36.6% in the Abstract ('Some 36.6% of respondents reported having transmitted misinformation at least once') and 36.3% in the Results. I kept 36.3% because it is internally consistent with the 63.7% 'never' figure given in the same sentence (100 - 63.7 = 36.3). Both are stated verbatim, so either satisfies R8; an adjudicator may prefer the abstract value.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) Table 1 subject shares (confinement and curfew 24.2%, political plot 17.2%, vaccine 16.6%, etc.) - these are the topic composition of misinformation examples among the 157 respondents who supplied an example, i.e. a breakdown inside an all-misinformation set, not a share of anything that could have been true; (b) 'The main source of misinformation was online news outlets (77.2%)' and Figure 4 - the composition of where respondents say they met misinformation, not a prevalence; (c) internet-use and platform-use figures (68.1% used the internet more, WhatsApp 74.2%, Instagram 72.2%, Facebook 64.4%, 64% naming social media as main information source) - exposure to information, not to misinformation; (d) the medical vs non-medical comparison (64.0% vs 63.4% claiming never to have spread misinformation; 3.1% of non-medical students at the highest frequency) is the paper's tested hypothesis but is reported only as the 'never' side, so extracting sharing rates by subgroup would require me to compute complements, which R8 forbids; (e) the 8.8% who reported meeting no misinformation is the complement of the 91.2% row. Figures 1-5 are images in the source PDF, so any values they carry beyond those quoted in the text were not readable.

rob.design: Descriptive cross-sectional online questionnaire (Google Forms) administered 8 March - 9 May 2021 to university students across Morocco via faculties and online student groups; convenience sample, no sampling frame and no response rate (303 questionnaires received, 8 excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria, 295 retained). Questionnaire validated on a pilot group of 10 respondents; no reliability statistics. Free-text misinformation examples were categorised by the authors into Political/Medical/Academic/Social subjects with no stated inter-coder agreement. Analysis is frequencies plus one chi-square test. The authors name the small sample as the study's limitation.

rob.item10_quote: The majority of respondents 269/295 (91.2%) claimed to have come across misinformation during the pandemic.
